title: Does growth follow the department instead?
question: Do agreements grow more in some departments than the kind of work would explain, so that a contractor effect can be told from a department effect?
finding: More clearly than it follows contractors. Among 18 departments with five or more measured agreements the share that grew by a quarter or more runs from 0% (Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development) to 86% (Homelessness and Supportive Housing). 3 of the 18 are above what their mix of work would give at the one-in-twenty level, where about 0.9 would be by chance: Public Health (95 of 129, 46% expected); Homelessness and Supportive Housing (49 of 57, 54% expected); Airport (26 of 42, 38% expected). For construction the only department figures are the Budget and Legislative Analyst's: across 297 construction contracts, July 1, 2021 to June 30, 2024, change orders added 8% to the first contract value, from 33% at Recreation and Park, 10% at Municipal Transportation Agency, 9% at Airport, 4% at Public Works, 3% at Port. The highest department is 11 times the lowest, a wider spread than anything these files show between contractors.
how: Board of Supervisors titles from 2014 to 2026 were linked into one record per agreement, following only links proven by a dollar figure carried from one title to the next or by a shared contract number (the rule used in the amendment-growth screen). The first amount is the total in the first approval on file or, where the first file is an amendment, the amount that amendment says it started from; the latest is the highest total approved. Left out: 527 leases and property; 225 no usable name in the title; 167 agreements with other public bodies; 164 no amount in any title; 58 loans; 21 agreements that bring money in (concessions, rents, franchises). For each department: agreements measured, the share that grew by a quarter or more, and the share expected if each agreement grew at the rate of the same kind of work in every other department. "Chance" is the probability of at least that many growing at those rates. The two contract-table tests (paid above the ceiling; paid two fiscal years after the end date) are shown where the Board's department code and the table's are the same. The last two columns are copied from Exhibit 1.13 of the Budget and Legislative Analyst's May 2026 audit of public works contracting: change orders as a share of the first contract value, by department.
limits: A department that buys services year after year (health, homelessness) will show more growth than one that buys equipment once, and sorting agreements into six kinds of work does not remove all of that. The Board-file rates cover only agreements large enough to need a Board vote. The official change-order shares cover three years and the analyst notes that the Airport funds design-build work in phases through change orders, which is why it adjusted the Airport figure; a small department with a few troubled projects (Recreation and Park) can show a high share on a small base. The project manager is not named in any file, so "the project manager's department" is the department that holds the contract. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
